h1: Fiberglass Insulation in San Leandro, CA
description: Fiberglass insulation in San Leandro, CA: batts and blown-in for attics and walls. Free inspection and a written estimate from East Bay Insulation.
intro: Fiberglass still does most of the insulating in East Bay homes, and for good reason: it delivers solid R-value per dollar in attics, walls and floors. We install batts and blown-in fiberglass, sealed and measured properly.
hero_alt: Fiberglass batts installed between attic joists

paragraphs: Batts suit open bays between joists and studs, where they can be cut tight around obstacles. Blown-in loose fill suits attics and hard-to-reach cavities, where it settles into every gap and covers uneven areas in one pass.
We recommend one over the other based on the space, not on habit: open attics usually get blown-in, wall cavities get batts or dense-pack.
bullets: Batts for open joist and stud bays
Blown-in for attics and irregular cavities
Depth markers so you can verify the R-value yourself

sections.h2: Installed right, not just laid down
paragraphs: Fiberglass performs when it is full-depth, dry and continuous. Gaps around pipes, wires and lights leak heat no matter how much material sits nearby.
Every fiberglass job includes the sealing work that makes the material count: top plates, penetrations, hatch weatherstripping and baffles at the soffits so airflow never gets blocked.

sections.h2: Where fiberglass fits in the East Bay
paragraphs: In open, dry attics with good access, blown-in fiberglass is usually the best value per R-value dollar. In rim joists, crawl spaces and anywhere moisture moves, we steer toward closed-cell foam or encapsulation instead, and explain why on the estimate.
The marine layer and cool nights mean even a modest R-value jump changes how the house feels, as long as the sealing is done alongside it.
Area, target R-value and access set the price: a tall attic costs less to work in than a low one, and topping up costs less than removing failed material first.
We quote the R-value, the depth and the square footage on paper, so you can compare bids on the same numbers.
bullets: Quoted by R-value and depth, not by truckload

paragraphs: Blown-in fiberglass settles slightly, which is why we install to a depth above the target, not at it. At the follow-up we re-check the depth and top off any areas that settled below the line.
You get a receipt showing the material, the R-value and the installed depth for your records and any future work.

steps.name: Inspection
steps.text: We measure the space and check the vents, sealing and existing material, then quote the right R-value for your house.
steps.image_alt: Measuring an attic for fiberglass insulation

steps.name: Seal and prep
steps.text: Leaks are sealed and baffles go in at the soffits so airflow stays clear when the material lands.

steps.name: Install
steps.text: Batts or blown-in fiberglass goes in to depth, with markers set at the target line.

steps.name: Check and top off
steps.text: We verify the depth with you and re-check at the follow-up visit after any settling.

faqs.q: Is fiberglass or cellulose better for my attic?
faqs.a: Both work. Fiberglass holds its loft in damp air and costs less per R-value in most attics, while cellulose packs tighter and blocks air a little better. We quote the option that fits your attic and your budget.
Most East Bay attics land between R-38 and R-60. The inspection tells us what your house has now and what it needs, and the estimate states the number.

faqs.q: How long does a fiberglass install take?
faqs.a: A standard attic is one day. Removal of old material or a large house can add a second day, stated in the estimate.
Blown-in fiberglass settles a little in the first months, so we install above the target depth and re-check at the follow-up visit.

faqs.q: Do you insulate walls with fiberglass?
faqs.a: Open stud bays get batts; finished walls get dense-pack blown-in through small access points. Both are standard jobs for us.
